title: NEW TAX RATES WILL SHOCK AMERICA IN 2027 — And Seniors Are The Target
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
The IRS has published the federal income tax brackets for 2027, and every number in them went
up. For somebody still working, that is good news.

If your income comes from Social Security, part of it moves the other way.

Your cost-of-living adjustment and the bracket adjustment are calculated from different things
at different times. When your benefit rises faster than the brackets do, more of your income
sits above a line than sat there last year. Nobody votes for that and nobody announces it.

And there is a second mechanism that reaches you and does not reach your children at all.

Whether your Social Security is taxable is decided by "provisional income" — your adjusted
gross income, plus tax-exempt interest, plus half your benefits — measured against $25,000 for
a single filer and $32,000 for a married couple. Those figures were set in 1983 and 1993 and
have never been adjusted for inflation. Not once. The second pair, $34,000 and $44,000, where
up to 85% of your benefit becomes taxable, has never moved either.

Everything else in the tax code is indexed every year. Those four numbers are not.

What this video covers:
- The official 2027 brackets, standard deduction, and the additional amount for age 65+
- How far the brackets moved, and how that compares with the 2027 COLA
- How to work out your own provisional income in five minutes, from two forms you already have
- The two thresholds, and what actually becomes taxable at each one
- Why "85% taxable" does not mean what most people think it means
- A worked example of somebody sitting exactly on the line
- Qualified charitable distributions, and why they never touch your AGI
- Roth conversions, and the one thing they permanently solve
- The Medicare connection — the same AGI sets your Part B premium two years later
- Three things that can still be done before December 31
- Why the new $6,000 senior deduction will NOT keep you under the threshold

Free help: IRS VITA and TCE (Tax Counseling for the Elderly, specifically for people over 60),
and AARP Foundation Tax-Aide. Both free, neither sells you anything. Find a site at irs.gov.

title: Every Senior Must Check This Before October 15 — The Medicare Switch You Cannot Undo

description:
Getting out of a Medicare Advantage plan is easy. Every year, from October fifteenth to
December seventh, you can leave and go back to Original Medicare, and nobody can stop you.

Buying a Medicare supplement afterwards is the part that can be refused.

Outside a short list of protected situations, an insurance company is allowed to look at
your health and turn you down, or charge you more. Medicare's own guide says it plainly:
"There's no guarantee that an insurance company will sell you a Medigap policy if you don't
meet their medical underwriting requirements."

That matters, because without a supplement you pay twenty percent of the Medicare-approved
amount and, in Medicare's words, "there's no yearly limit on what you pay out of pocket."

But there is a list of situations where the company has no choice at all - where it must
sell to you, must cover conditions you already have, and cannot ask a single medical
question. Most of the people on that list have no idea they are on it. This video walks
through all fifteen, biggest first.

What this video covers:
The twelve-month trial right, and the rule that lets you leave on ANY day of the year
The sixty-three day clock inside it that quietly costs people the right they earned

title: Don't Give Your House to Your Kids to Protect It From the Nursing Home — Do This Instead
views_per_day_limitation: Snapshot views divided by age at retrieval; not a historical velocity series.
description:
Putting your house in your children's names to keep it safe from a nursing home feels like the smart, loving move. It is one of the most common — and most expensive — mistakes older homeowners make, and it can backfire three ways at once. First, the tax trap: gifting a home during your life means your kids take your original purchase price as their tax basis, so when they sell they can owe capital gains on decades of appreciation — a home bought for $50,000 and worth $400,000 could hand them a $50,000+ tax bill that inheriting it would have erased through the stepped-up basis. Second, your home becomes exposed to your child's creditors, lawsuits, bankruptcy, and divorce — a court can force its sale for a debt that was never yours. Third, gifting the home within five years of applying for Medicaid triggers a penalty, so it often fails to protect the home anyway. The better way: a lady bird deed (enhanced life estate deed) or a transfer-on-death deed lets the home pass to your children at your death, outside probate, while you keep full control for life — with no gift tax return, no Medicaid penalty, and the stepped-up basis preserved. Talk to an elder law or estate planning attorney before you add a single name to your deed.

For general information only. This is not legal or tax advice. A lady bird deed is not available in every state and the rules vary. Talk with a qualified elder law or estate planning attorney about your own home, state, and family.
